title: Argentina's World Cup Defence: Can the Champions Do It Again?
summary: Winning a World Cup is extraordinary. Defending it is something only Brazil in 1962 has managed. With Messi in what will surely be his final tournament, can Argentina write history twice?
content:
When Lionel Messi lifted the World Cup trophy in Lusail at the end of the 2022 final — one of the greatest football matches ever played, settled in a penalty shootout against France after a 3-3 draw — it completed a career story that had seemed for years to be building toward tragedy. The best player in the history of the sport winning the only trophy that had eluded him. The completeness was almost too perfect.

In 2026, Argentina return to defend that trophy. And Messi, now 38, will almost certainly be making his final World Cup appearance. The story is not over.

The Weight of History

Only one nation has successfully defended the World Cup in the modern era: Brazil in 1958 and 1962, in an era when the competition was structurally different and the gap between elite South American football and the rest of the world was wider than it is today. The tournament's format, its physical demands across a month of competitive football, and the degree of focus that every opponent brings to matches against the champion make successful defence almost impossibly difficult.

Argentina know this. The coaching staff have discussed it openly. The mental challenge — playing every match knowing that the opponent has nothing to lose against you — requires a different preparation than the 2022 campaign that produced the title. The team that won Qatar may no longer be the team best suited to defending it.

The Squad Evolution

Four years have passed. Some of the players who were central to 2022 are older in ways that matter at the highest level. Others have grown into their peak years. Argentina's squad for 2026 is not the same squad that won in Qatar — it has evolved, refreshed in some positions, deepened in others.

The question of how much the team can function without Messi — not because he will not be there, but because building dependence on a 38-year-old for a month-long tournament is a risk — has shaped the coaching staff's approach to the younger generation. Players who might previously have deferred to Messi's decisions on the pitch have been encouraged to take more responsibility. The team needs to be functional without him, even as it benefits from him when he is at his best.

I will give everything I have for Argentina for as long as I am playing. This tournament is special for me in a way I cannot fully explain. After what we achieved in 2022, I want to show that it was not just one moment. That this team can achieve great things consistently. — Lionel Messi

The Competition

The 2026 World Cup field is deeper than 2022's, partly because of the expansion to 48 teams and partly because the genuine talent available to leading football nations has never been broader. France, Brazil, England, Germany, Spain — all of them have assembled squads that are capable of winning. The defence will not be conducted against weaker opposition.

What Would It Mean?

If Argentina win in 2026 — if Messi lifts a second World Cup at 38, in what may be his final competitive match — it would be one of the most remarkable achievements in the history of sport. Not just because of what it would mean statistically, not just because of the difficulty of defending a World Cup, but because of the narrative completeness: the greatest player of his generation, retiring as a two-time world champion, in a tournament hosted by a country where his sport has found its newest audience.

It is possible. It is not the probability. But in football, as in sport more broadly, the improbable is often what we remember longest.
